content: Toluene, also referred to as methylbenzene or phenylmethane, is a transparent liquid that does not dissolve in water. It has a characteristic odor reminiscent of paint thinners, with a sweet smell similar to benzene. It is classified as an aromatic hydrocarbon and is extensively utilized in industrial applications as a feedstock and solvent. The term toluene originates from the older name toluol, which was derived from tolu balsam, an aromatic extract obtained from the tropical Colombian tree Myroxylon balsamum. Toluene was first isolated from this source and was originally named by the chemist Jöns Jakob Berzelius. Chemically, toluene behaves as a typical aromatic hydrocarbon in electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions. The presence of the methyl group makes it approximately 25 times more reactive than benzene in such reactions. For instance, toluene undergoes sulfonation to produce para-toluenesulfonic acid and chlorination in the presence of FeCl₃ to yield orthoand para-chlorotoluene isomers. Nitration of toluene results in orthoand para-nitrotoluene isomers, and under heating, it can form dinitrotoluene and eventually trinitrotoluene (TNT), an explosive compound. The methyl side chain of toluene is also reactive and can undergo oxidation. For example, oxidation with potassium permanganate produces benzoic acid, while reaction with chromyl chloride yields benzaldehyde (via the Étard reaction). Halogenation can occur under free radical conditions, such as when toluene reacts with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) in the presence of AIBN, forming benzyl bromide. Catalytic hydrogenation of toluene to methylcyclohexane requires high hydrogen pressure due to the stability of the aromatic ring. The pKa of toluene is approximately 45. Toluene is naturally present in small amounts in crude oil and is typically produced during processes such as catalytic reforming in gasoline production, ethylene cracking, or coke production from coal. Final separation of toluene is achieved in BTX plants through distillation or solvent extraction. Toluene is a widely used solvent capable of dissolving substances such as paints, paint thinners, chemical reactants, rubber, printing inks, adhesives, lacquers, leather tanners, and disinfectants. It is also employed as a fullerene indicator and serves as a raw material for the production of toluene diisocyanate (used in polyurethane foam manufacturing) and TNT. Industrially, toluene is used in processes such as dealkylation to produce benzene and disproportionation to yield a mixture of benzene and xylene. Oxidation of toluene produces benzaldehyde and benzoic acid, which are important intermediates in chemical synthesis. Additionally, toluene is used as a carbon source for synthesizing multi-wall carbon nanotubes. In biochemistry experiments, toluene can be utilized to lyse red blood cells for hemoglobin extraction. It is also employed as an octane booster in gasoline for internal combustion engines. Notably, in the 1980s, Formula 1 turbo engines were fueled with gasoline containing 84% toluene by volume. In terms of toxicology and metabolism, inhalation of toluene fumes can cause intoxication, and at higher doses, it may induce nausea. Toluene can enter the human body not only through vapor inhalation but also via soil contamination, where exposure may occur through contact with contaminated soil, ingestion of polluted groundwater, or inhalation of soil vapor emissions. The toxicity of toluene is primarily attributed to its metabolism. Due to its low water solubility, toluene cannot be excreted through conventional routes such as urine, feces, or sweat. Instead, it must undergo metabolic transformation for elimination. The methyl group in toluene is more readily oxidized by cytochrome P450 enzymes than the benzene ring. Consequently, approximately 95% of toluene is metabolized to benzyl alcohol. The remaining 5% is oxidized to benzaldehyde and cresols, which are toxic metabolites. Most reactive products are detoxified through conjugation with glutathione, but residual metabolites can cause significant cellular damage. Toluene is primarily excreted as benzoic acid and hippuric acid, both of which are formed through further metabolic oxidation of benzyl alcohol.
